titleStmt.title: Towards a Descriptive Language to Explicitly Define the Applicability of Timing Verification Tests of Critical Real-Time Systems

analytic.title: Towards a Descriptive Language to Explicitly Define the Applicability of Timing Verification Tests of Critical Real-Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Real-time systems are used in many critical domains such as automotive, avionics and nuclear, therefore their temporal behavior needs to be checked rigorously. Many scheduling theory-based analysis tests have been proposed to validate the design of real-time systems. Since each given test is based on a set of assumptions, only the constrained system which satisfies these assumptions can be reliably verified by such a test. These assumptions do not depend on any design language but their interpretation does. Currently, these assumptions are often drowned in scientific paper discussions and expressed in natural languages. In this paper, we aim to make possible to define formally assumptions by real-time systems analysts without being expert of design languages. Indeed, we propose a domain specific language named IRL (Identification Rule Language). We show the benefit of such a language to capitalize efforts. That is, IRL allows to define analysis supports to help the timing verification community to share its knowledge and enables systems designers to use this knowledge easily.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: A Real-Time System (RTS) is a set of hardware execution nodes (e.g., processors and buses) and software components (e.g., tasks, processes and messages) cooperating to accomplish a set of specific missions constrained by timing requirements. The correct behaviour of RTS depends not only on the logical result of software functionality, but also on the moments when the results are produced. RTS are used in many critical domains such as avionics, automotive and nuclear. That is, a failure of RTS can seriously impact many human lives and the environment. Moreover, the development process of safety-critical RTS takes several months up to years. Therefore, RTS designs should be validated at an early design phase by checking if all temporal requirements are met, otherwise the time-to-market can be sharply impacted. The timing verification of RTS consists in proving that the system will always be able to react in accordance with its timing constraints (i.e. deadline, endto-end latency, etc.). The timing verification of RTS can be checked thanks to simulations, formal methods (i.e., model checking applied to Petri-net or timed automata), or algebraic methods based on the scheduling theory [1], [2] (like the processor utilization factor, the demand bound function, response time analysis, etc.). Scheduling analysis tests are very popular in critical system domains since they are scalable and they have been implemented in different academic [3], [4], [5] and commercial tools [6], [7], [8]. Also, they allow to dimension RTS during the design and to avoid over-sizing especially in case of embedded systems.

Numerous schedulability analysis have been proposed since the 1970s to deal with different kinds of RTS due to the evolution of the hardware components and software architectures. In fact, every analysis test is related to a specific application situation (i.e., a set of assumptions related to the software and hardware architecture of the analyzed systems) within which test results are valid. In the rest of the paper we call context the set of assumptions required for an analysis test to be applicable. That is, the result of an analysis test can never be reliable unless the system fits accurately with the context of the applied test.

Nowadays, thanks to model-driven engineering [9], the design of RTS has been shortened. Several modeling languages have been proposed [10], [11], [12]. Also several analysis tools can be used after transforming the design to their input formalism. However, we notice the gap between RTS analysis community and modellers community still exists since only few analysis tests proposed by the academic analyst researchers are used in the industry. That is due to the existence of a multitude of tests scattered in different articles and whose usage requires a strong knowledge about the system configuration (e.g., the scheduling policy, hardware architecture, communication patterns, etc.) and on the schedulability analysis. Therefore, the RTS designers have to be sure that the chosen analysis tests for their systems hold in their contexts.

Recently, several studies are capitalizing efforts of analysis related to the timing verification [13], [14], [15] by helping, on the one hand, RTS designers to find and to use easily analysis tests that correspond to their needs. On the other hand, this capitalization relies on helping analysts (especially academic community) to share their proposed analysis tests and easing the reuse of their prototypes. That also allows enhancing the applicability of the academic scheduling analysis tests. In this perspective, the contribution of this paper represents a part of a large project. Indeed, the objective of this paper is to make contexts of analysis tests machine-interpretable by providing a descriptive language close to the analysts domain and its technical jargon, then to enable analysts to share their knowledge through an analysis repository. This latter should be used by designers and play the role of a decision support to choose appropriate applicable tests.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the background and the work positioning. Section III presents the foundations of the descriptive language and its usage. Section IV is dedicated to the discussions and proof of concept. Finally, Section V concludes this paper.

div.head: A. Running and motivation example
div.p: The assumptions characterizing the contexts are sometimes well defined in the scientific papers (as in the seminal work [16] presented in Figure 1), and sometimes they are drowned in the paper discussions as it is shown by the underlined sentences of Figure 2 or even left implicit. Unfortunately, the second case is very common. The drowned assumptions of Figure 2 correspond to the Response Time Analysis (RTA) test dedicated to sporadic independent tasks [17] executed on a single processor architecture. These assumptions have been extracted from three different parts of this research. The bottom part of Figure 2 shows the algebraic formula corresponding to the RTA test (which is presented in another section of [17]).

Moreover, even if some papers present explicitly the assumptions sometimes the generalization of tests to support other contexts by reinforcing assumptions or by relaxing them, remains implicit (as shown by the underlined sentence of Figure 1). Furthermore, although the assumptions can be explicitly listed, sometimes they lack accuracy. For instance, the assumption "single processor" shown in Figure 2 does not precise if the processor contains a cache-memory or not. This was not lacking in embedded systems in 1994, but due to to the evolution of the hardware architecture, it is lacking in the 21 st century. In fact, the test has been proposed in 1994 where the cache memories were not used in critical RTS.

Besides, note that an analysis test can be related to many contexts with different importance levels. In the literature, we find three levels [1]: sufficient condition, necessary condition and exact condition.

For all these reasons, to choose the right analysis for a safety-critical RTS, the conventional current solution is to ask an expert. Nevertheless, since our objective is to make designers more autonomous, it would be good to have a test analysis repository gathering efforts of experts and also helping to clarify the contexts of the analysis on an accurate and unified way. Our mid-term objective is also to help RTS analysis community to enhance the sharing and reuse of new analysis tests (proposed in conferences and journals) and also to manage the evolution of the assumptions.

div.head: B. Background and work positioning
div.p: Y. Ouhammou et al. proposed [18] the framework MoSaRT (Modeling-oriented Scheduling analysis of Real-Time systems) whose front-end is MoSaRT Design Language and whose back-end is an Analysis Repository (A rep ) defined in [18] as follows: A rep = <R, C, T > where,

• T = {t 1 , t 2 , .., t n } is a set of analysis tests proposed in the literature; • R = {r 1 , r 2 , .., r n } is the union of all assumptions defining C. The evaluation result of a rule can be true or false depending on the evaluated context that the rule defines. R is also called a repository of identification rules since this latter allows to identify tests matching a given RTS design.
div.formula: • C = {c 1 , c 2 , .., c n } is a set of contexts (applica- tions domains of test), such that every context c i = < R true i , R f alse i , R indif i , T i > where R true i
div.p: is a subset of R containing the rules which should be true in the context, R f alse i is a subset of R containing the rules which should be false in the context, R indif i is a subset of R containing the rules whose value can be either true or false and
div.formula: R true i ∪ R f alse i ∪ R indif i = R
div.p: and T i is a subset of analysis tests ⊂ T that can be applied when a RTS design matches the context. A rep is based on OCL (Object Constraint Language) [19] with MoSaRT Design Language concepts. Basically, OCL is used to reinforce meta-models semantics by adding a set of constraints, hence to check the conformity of models referring to their meta-models, but Y. Ouhammou et al. used OCL to express assumptions (i.e., identification rules) to help designers to choose the appropriate tests for their systems expressed in MoSaRT Design Language. Although OCL provides a predicate expressive syntax enabling to express exactly constraints and assumptions, its weakness to express rules in A rep is that OCL depends on a set of concepts and properties of the target design language (e.g., AADL [11], Time4Sys [20], MARTE [12]), MoSaRT [18]). Therefore the one who writes the assumptions has to master not only OCL syntax but also the meta-model structure of the target design language. Listing 1 shows an example of an assumption expressed in OCL with AADL concepts. Example of an assumption expressed in OCL for AADL Nguyen et al. [13] have proposed a framework called PARAD (Performance Analysis Repository for AADL Design) based on REAL (Requirement Enforcement Analysis Language) [21]. REAL is a constraint language that provides a simple syntax close to the natural language.

Nevertheless, the utilization of REAL is restricted to RTS designs expressed in AADL [11]. Moreover, REAL provides only "foreach" statement to iterate a set of AADL components which is equivalent to universal quantifier (i.e., for all), but it does not provide the existential quantifier (i.e., exist).

Another limitation of existing works is related to the evolution of modeling languages. That is, since the RTS domain is evolving continuously and identification rules are expressed in a formalism based on a specific version of a given modeling language, each evolution in terms of the meta-model structure and concepts (of such a modeling language) impacts the identification rules that are already stored in the analysis repository. In other words, the evolution of a modeling language requires to update the analysis repository to be compliant with the new version. This process is timeconsuming.

For all the reasons presented previously, this paper proposes a DSL (domain specific language) dedicated to RTS analysts. The DSL should be independent of existing modeling languages. The idea behind this DSL is not to create a new constraint language like OCL or REAL, but we aim at creating a pivot language, on which, the end-user (academic researchers and practitioner analysts) can define easily and accurately the assumptions without mastering OCL or the target modeling language.

To make this paper self-contained and to more clarify its contribution, Figure 3 presents an overview of the whole framework workflow including the part related to the current contribution. Let us look first at the RTS modellers who can design their systems conforming to a given modeling language such as MARTE [12], Time4Sys [20], AADL [11] or MoSaRT [18]. Depending on these latters, modellers would seek in a compliant analysis repository to find most appropriate analysis tests for their system designs. The adapted analysis repository shall contain the same content as the generic analysis repository, except the identification rules which should be transformed and expressed in a language compliant to the modeling language (e.g. OCL or REAL). Thus, the paper contribution consists in formulating accurately the analysis tests and their contexts, and then feeding the generic analysis repository. This latter can be transformed, if needed, to be compliant with one or several languages.

div.head: III. TOWARDS GENERIC ANALYSIS REPOSITORIES
div.p: In this section, we firstly propose a pivot description language called Identification Rule Language (IRL) dedicated to express the contexts in order to be machine-interpretable, then they will be reusable. Secondly, we present the extension of the analysis repository meta-model in order to define repositories independently of any RTS modeling language.

div.head: A. Identification Rule Description Language
div.p: The simplest model that allows to define assumptions is the propositional logic. For example, "The system has mono-processor architecture" is a proposition. However, the propositional logic has several limitations. One key limitation is that there is no way to talk about properties that apply to categories of subjects. For example "it exists at least n tasks whose response time is lower than the deadline", is an assumption that cannot be expressed using Figure 3. Analysis repository usage's workflow the propositional logic. Thus, the predicate logic is more expressive than the propositional logic. The main difference is that predicate logic contrarily to the propositional logic contains quantifiers (i.e., existential quantifier and universal quantifier) and allows to work with variables. For the reasons mentioned above, we are inspired by the predicate logic paradigm to formalize the identification rule language.

We recall that the objective is not to propose yet another implementation of the first-order logic (like OCL or DLdescription logic [22] which is mainly used in knowledgebased and ontology engineering domains). Surely, it is better to design a small language that is highly expressive (precise, concise, readable), because it focuses on a specific narrow domain [23]. Thus, since IRL is a domain specific language, in the following we present its abstract syntax (meta-model).

Figure 4 shows an excerpt of the IRL meta-model (expressed in Ecore [24]) where classes in a grey color are abstract classes. The meta-model contains two parts. While the first part (Part A of Figure 4) describes the structure of predicates which is fixed, the second part (Part B of Figure 4) is evolutive and is dedicated to real-time concepts used in predicates.

1) Predicate part of the meta-model: the central element of the first part of the IRL language is the Expression class. Every assumption is an identification rule based on a predicate logic expression (instance of Expression class as shown in Figure 4). It is composed of a sequence of variables (instances of Variable) and a proposition (instance of Proposition class).

Each instance of Variable class is characterized by the quantifier attribute (∃ or ∀) and a name. A variable can have a basic primitive type (i.e., real or integer) as it is illustrated by NaturalInteger and Real classes which inherit from the PredefinedSet abstract class. A variable may also be an element of real-time ComponentType (will be presented later). A variable can also be an element of a customized set, where every customized set is an instance of UserDefinedDomain class.

Each Proposition has an operator. An operator can be a customized function as an instance of BinaryFunction class or UnaryFunction class. Otherwise, the operator is an instance of BasicArithmeticOperator class (e.g., addition, subtraction, etc.). Depending on the function type used, a proposition has one or several operands (instances of Operand class). An operand can be an instance of the following classes: Constant, real-time PropertyValue, Proposition or Accessor. Each instance of Accessor class references an element of ReferenceableElement abstract class. Then, the referenceable element can be a Variable, a PredefinedSet or a UserDefinedDomain.

2) Evolutive part of the meta-model: while our objective is to get a pivot language independent of any design language, we have opted to separate the meta-model into two parts. That will ensure the evolution of concepts used in real-time systems then to follow continuously the progress of RTS domain. In this perspective and contrarily to other standard modeling languages which are prescriptive models, we would like to make the second part of the IRL meta-model descriptive [25]. Hence, we have conceived the second part as an RTS domain ontology.

In the best of our knowledge, it does not exist any consensual ontology for RTS domain. We have focused on the scheduling-aware concepts of RTS domain. Actually, this ontology contains more than 90 concepts classified in three categories. (i) ComponentType category which contains most entities used in RTS. (ii) PropertyType category which deals with grouping common RTS properties used for timing verification. (iii) The value of every element of PropertyType category can be either literal value or an element from the PropertyValue group.

div.head: B. Analysis repository meta-model extension
div.p: In order to face the limitations of the analysis repository A rep structure presented in Section II, especially the impossibility to express assumptions independently from the design language, we propose the extension illustrated in Figure 5. Thanks to this extension, analysis repositories (instance of the extended meta-model) will be generic. Indeed, the formal expression of IdentificationRule class will be expressed in IRL instead of using REAL or OCL.
Figure 5 presents the extension of Identification Rule to express formally the assumptions.

div.head: IV. PROOF OF CONCEPT
div.p: This section highlights the usefulness of Identification Rule Language and also the extension of MoSaRT analysis repository meta-model leading to get generic analysis repositories.

1) Tooling: IRL has been implemented as a plugin of Eclipse IDE [26]. Then, in order to express assumptions with IRL, two concrete syntaxes can be used. The first one is a textual syntax close to the natural language. This syntax is developed thanks to Xtext tool [27]. Figure 6 presents The shown grammar is related to Expression class (of Figure 5).

For instance, the assumption meaning that "for all tasks of a given RTS, each task period is greater or equal to the task deadline" is illustrated by Figure 6 showing an Expression instance with a variable and a proposition. The variable is characterized by forAll quantifier, its name is "t" and it is an element from "Task" set. The proposition is an instance of BooleanProposition class. It is composed of a main operator greater or equal (i.e., >=) and two arguments. Each argument has an instance of GetProperty The second concrete syntax is the default EMF (Eclipse Modeling Framework [28]) tree diagram. It enables to get synthetic view of instantiated assumptions.
Note that, the new version of MoSaRT analysis repository (the extended meta-model) has been also developed using Xtext tool as shown hereafter.

2) Example: Figure 7 presents an example of the generic analysis repository containing three analysis tests collected from three scientific papers. We have chosen three kinds of analysis: a validation test (i.e., Response Time Analysis [17]), a dimensioning test (i.e., Optimal Priority Analysis [29]) and a sensitivity analysis test (i.e., [30]). These tests are related to three different periods (1980s, 1990s and 2000s).

The repository contains 12 assumptions, each one is characterized by an id, a description and a formal expression. Note that those assumptions have been added into repository progressively. The number of assumptions in scientific papers progresses with the evolution of software and hardware architectures.

3) Discussion: Currently, the instantiating of the analysis repository has been done by us. We plan to integrate the tool as a teaching aid-tool in master courses especially in "modeling and analysis of real-time embedded systems" course. Our long-term objective is to enhance the maturity of the proposed approach in order to be used as a support of artifact evaluation in RTS domain's conference (like in https://rtns2018.ensma.fr/artifactevaluation.html). Thanks to the usage of analysis repositories in several collaborative projects, we have detected several points that can be improved.

• Due to the large number of identification rules existing in an analysis repository, it is a possibility to have some redundant rules. • It is possible to have some rules included in others since it is possible to write formal expressions with "and" and "or" operators.
• We have noticed that the description of a context requires to skim all existing rules. This process depends on the number of rules and it can require non-negligible effort.
• Basically, the analysis repository should be fed by experts, but it would be useful to help them in order to check the consistency of each context description.

For instance, conflicting assumptions should not exist together in the description of a context. To cope with these issues, we are working on reinforcing our modeling framework by a set of formal verification tools dedicated to check the atomicity of a rule and to detect duplicated rules.

We are also working on adding semantic relationships (equivalence, refinement, requirement, contradiction) between rules in order to check the consistency of contexts and to infer other possible relationships between both contexts and rules.

V. CONCLUSION Timing verification of critical real-time systems is an important and crucial phase of the development life-cycle. Due to the complexity of new RTS architectures and due to the existence of a plethora of tests, the timing verification is error-prone and time consuming. In this paper, we presented the Identification Rule Language (IRL) as a pivot language based on the predicate logic in order to capitalize efforts of expert analysts. That is thanks to IRL and the generic analysis repositories, knowledge and expertise required for the timing verification can be stored in a machine-interpretable way. That allows also researchers to share their test to be used by designers who are not necessarily experts in timing verification. In fact, thanks to this work, RTS designers will be supported since their models can be systematically checked by one or several analysis repositories.
